Overview

One tool. The complete picture.

Atlas connects to your environment over SSH, MongoDB, Redis, and the Platform API — collecting data, running it through a curated ruleset, and handing you a clear report.

Capture

Connects via SSH, MongoDB, Redis-py, and the Platform API to collect configuration data from every component of your deployment.

Validate

Runs captured data through over 100 best-practice rules covering Redis, MongoDB, Platform, and Gateway at critical, warning, and info severity.

Report

Generates interactive HTML compliance reports with filterable findings, severity breakdowns, and pass/fail scores across all subsystems.

Platform Atlas · v2.0

Your IAP deployment,
audited and understood.

Platform Atlas connects to your Itential Automation Platform environment, collects configuration data from every component, validates it against a set of best-practice rules, and generates professional compliance reports — across either a quick application-only audit or the full infrastructure sweep, with an optional browser-based companion.

Standard · SaaS · Extended tiers Up to 108 validation rules Continuous drift monitoring Optional WebUI

What is Platform Atlas?

Platform Atlas is a configuration auditing tool built specifically for the Itential Automation Platform. Think of it as a knowledgeable colleague who knows exactly what a healthy IAP deployment looks like — it reads your configuration, checks it against a curated ruleset, and hands you a clear report showing what's right, what needs attention, and why.

Capture

Pick a tier — Standard hits Platform OAuth and the Gateway 4 API only; SaaS audits a single standalone Gateway 4 or 5; Extended adds SSH, MongoDB, Redis, and Kubernetes. Same workflow either way.

Validate

~55 rules in Standard, ~108 in Extended, just the chosen gateway's rules in SaaS. Rules that need data outside the active tier are SKIPped, never counted against the score.

Report & Monitor

Three HTML reports per session (one merged report in SaaS), plus optional Continuous Audit that re-runs on a schedule and pings Slack/webhooks when rules drift.

Atlas is designed for both Itential Customer Success teams running quarterly health checks and customers who want to perform self-service validation at any time. Once you're set up, a full audit is just two commands: create a session, then run it. v2.0 also ships an optional WebUI companion package that exposes the same workflow in a local-only browser interface — see the section below.

Standard, SaaS & Extended Tiers

Atlas ships with three audit modes. Standard and Extended are global settings you pick once; SaaS is chosen per-environment at create time. Sessions remember the tier they were created under, so cross-tier comparisons stay honest.

Standard

~55 rules. Platform OAuth + Gateway 4 API only. No SSH, no MongoDB, no Redis. Set up in five minutes if you have a Platform URI and OAuth credentials.

Use it for quick application-layer audits, environments where infrastructure access is restricted, or as a pre-flight before requesting full Extended access.

SaaS (new in v2.0)

Gateway rules only. Audits one standalone Gateway 4 or Gateway 5 — no Platform, MongoDB, or Redis anywhere in the flow. GW4 over its REST API with optional SSH; GW5 over SSH printenv or a local Compose/Helm file.

Chosen during env create and fixed for that environment's lifetime. Produces a single merged report (compliance + Architecture Overview).

Extended

~108 rules. Full infrastructure: SSH into every server, MongoDB and Redis configuration, Kubernetes via kubectl, Gateway 4 / 5. Default for upgrades from 1.6.x.

Use it for formal quarterly health assessments and any environment where you have the credentials and access needed.

# Inspect or change the active tier
platform-atlas tier show
platform-atlas tier set standard
platform-atlas tier set extended

# SaaS is per-environment — pick it in the create wizard
platform-atlas env create

# Override per-command without touching the persisted setting
platform-atlas --tier standard preflight
DefaultsFresh installs start in Standard. Upgrades from 1.6.x stay on Extended automatically — nothing changes in your existing workflow unless you opt in. SaaS is never a global default and never a conversion target — a SaaS environment keeps its tier and gateway kind for life.

Requirements

Atlas is a Python CLI tool that runs on the machine you use to connect to your IAP environment — typically your workstation or a jump host with network access to your servers. What you need depends on which tier you'll run.

Always required

  • Python 3.11 or later
  • A Platform OAuth service account with read-only API access (apiread:Adapters, apiread:Health, etc.)
  • An OS keyring backend, or HashiCorp Vault with a KV v2 secrets engine

Standard tier — only the above

If you only intend to run Standard audits, you're done. No SSH or database credentials needed.

SaaS tier — gateway credentials instead of Platform

A SaaS audit needs no Platform OAuth account at all. For Gateway 4: the gateway's API URL, username, and password — plus SSH access to the gateway host if you opt into the deeper SSH checks. For Gateway 5: SSH to the gateway host, or just a local copy of its Docker Compose / Helm values file (no server access needed).

Extended tier — additional

  • SSH access to your IAP, MongoDB, and Redis nodes (key-based authentication recommended)
  • A MongoDB user with clusterMonitor on admin and read on the Platform database
  • A Redis user with +config|get, +info, +acl, +ping, +role ACL permissions

If direct SSH to any server is blocked (CyberArk PSMP, etc.), use ControlMaster transport — see the ControlMaster section of this guide. ControlMaster can be applied to any node (IAP, MongoDB, Redis, Gateway) independently. If Atlas itself is installed on the Platform server, use the Local transport for the IAP node and SSH for everything else.

Install on your workstationAtlas works best installed on a workstation PC that has remote access to your IAP environment. It doesn't need to be on the same machine as IAP itself.

Installation

Atlas ships as a Python wheel file (.whl) provided by your Itential contact. The fastest way to get set up is the install script — it handles everything for you. If you prefer to do it manually or need to work in a locked-down environment, the manual steps are right below it.

Option A — Use the install script (recommended)

The install scripts live in the install_scripts/ folder at the root of your Atlas package. They check your Python version, create a virtual environment in a location you choose, install Atlas (and optionally the WebUI), and wire up your shell so platform-atlas works from any terminal — without you having to remember to activate anything.

The scripts don't install anything system-wide and don't need root or administrator access. Everything goes into a single folder (~/atlas_venv by default) that you can delete at any time to completely remove Atlas.

macOS and Linux

Open a terminal, navigate to the folder that contains both the install script and the wheel file(s), and run:

# Place the wheel file(s) in the same directory as the script and run:
bash install_scripts/linux-mac_install.sh

The script will walk you through every step. If it finds the wheel file automatically you won't need to type anything until it asks where to install.

You can also pass paths directly to skip the prompts. Use --webui to install the optional WebUI alongside the CLI:

bash install_scripts/linux-mac_install.sh --wheel ~/Downloads/platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
# CLI + WebUI together:
bash install_scripts/linux-mac_install.sh --wheel ~/Downloads/platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl --webui ~/Downloads/platform_atlas_webui-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

Windows

Open PowerShell (you don't need administrator mode), navigate to the folder with the script and wheel file(s), and run:

# You may need to allow local scripts on first run
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser

.\install_scripts\windows_install.ps1

The script prompts you for everything it needs. Use -Wheel and -WebUI flags to pass paths directly:

.\install_scripts\windows_install.ps1 -Wheel .\platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
# CLI + WebUI together:
.\install_scripts\windows_install.ps1 -Wheel .\platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl -WebUI .\platform_atlas_webui-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

Option B — Manual install

If you'd rather do it yourself, or if the script doesn't fit your environment, here's the same process step by step.

Step 1 — Check your Python version

Atlas requires Python 3.11 or newer. Check what you have:

python3 --version
# or try: python --version

You need to see Python 3.11.x or higher. If you see 3.9, 3.10, or anything older, install a newer version first.

OSHow to install Python 3.11+
macOSbrew install python@3.11 — or download from python.org
RHEL 9 / Rocky 9sudo dnf install python3.11 python3.11-pip
RHEL 8 / Rocky 8sudo dnf module enable python311 && sudo dnf install python311
Ubuntu / Debiansudo apt install python3.11 python3.11-venv (add deadsnakes PPA if not found)
WindowsMicrosoft Store → search "Python 3.11", or download from python.org (tick "Add to PATH")

Step 2 — Create a virtual environment

A virtual environment keeps Atlas isolated from other Python tools on your system. You only do this once.

# macOS / Linux — creates the environment at ~/atlas_venv
python3.11 -m venv ~/atlas_venv

# Windows (PowerShell)
python -m venv $env:USERPROFILE\atlas_venv

Step 3 — Activate and install

# macOS / Linux
source ~/atlas_venv/bin/activate
pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:USERPROFILE\atlas_venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl

Step 4 — Verify and make it permanent

# Verify the install
platform-atlas --version

# macOS / Linux — add the venv to your PATH so it's always available
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/atlas_venv/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc   # or ~/.zshrc
source ~/.bashrc

On Windows, add %USERPROFILE%\atlas_venv\Scripts to your user PATH in Settings → System → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables.

✓
You're installed. You should see a version string like platform-atlas 2.0.0. If you get "command not found", make sure you've either added the venv to your PATH (step 4) or that the virtual environment is active.

Troubleshooting common install problems

ProblemMost likely cause and fix
command not found: platform-atlas The virtual environment isn't active and its bin/ folder isn't on your PATH. Either run source ~/atlas_venv/bin/activate first, or add ~/atlas_venv/bin to your PATH permanently (see Step 4 above).
python3: command not found or wrong version Try python3.11, python3.12, or py -3 (Windows). If none work, Python 3.11+ isn't installed yet — see the table in Step 1.
pip: No module named pip The venv was created without pip. Delete the venv folder and recreate with python3.11 -m venv --upgrade-deps ~/atlas_venv.
ERROR: platform_atlas requires Python >=3.11 The venv was created with an older Python. Check which Python the venv uses: ~/atlas_venv/bin/python --version. Delete the venv and recreate with python3.11.
Works in terminal, not in a new window (macOS/Linux) The PATH change wasn't picked up. Run source ~/.bashrc or source ~/.zshrc, or close and reopen the terminal.
PowerShell says "running scripts is disabled" Run: Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser — this only affects your own account and is safe.

Headless Linux: credential storage

On a headless Linux server without a desktop environment, the OS keyring often has nowhere to securely store a secret. Atlas handles this automatically: if the keyring can't be used, it falls back to its built-in encrypted local file store at ~/.atlas/credentials.enc — so setup and capture just work, with no manual configuration. The file is encrypted with AES-256-GCM keyed to this host and user plus a random per-install salt (~/.atlas/.keysalt), so it won't decrypt if copied to another machine, and a single leaked file is useless without the salt. This covers both keyring and Vault mode (in Vault mode it's the Vault connection settings that move to the file). Atlas reports honestly — in preflight, config doctor, and the banner — whenever the file store is active.

You can also force the file store explicitly, which is handy if automatic detection doesn't engage on an unusual host:

platform-atlas config credentials --use-file-store   # switch this host to the encrypted file store
platform-atlas config credentials --auto             # revert to keyring-first (automatic)

For server fleets, HashiCorp Vault remains an excellent option — it keeps secrets centrally managed and out of any local store. And if you specifically want an encrypted OS keyring on the server instead, you can still select one by hand:

source ~/atlas_venv/bin/activate
pip install keyring keyrings.alt pycryptodome

# Option A: per-shell (add to ~/.bashrc to persist)
export PYTHON_KEYRING_BACKEND=keyrings.alt.file.EncryptedKeyring

# Option B: configure the encrypted file keyring globally
mkdir -p ~/.config/python_keyring
cat > ~/.config/python_keyring/keyringrc.cfg <<EOF
[backend]
default-keyring=keyrings.alt.file.EncryptedKeyring
EOF

With the manual keyring option you'll be prompted for a keyring passphrase the first time Atlas stores a credential.

Optional: WebUI companion package

A second wheel — platform_atlas_webui-*.whl — adds a browser-based interface alongside the CLI. Install it into the same virtual environment:

source ~/atlas_venv/bin/activate   # skip if already active
pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas_webui-1.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
platform-atlas-webui

The WebUI shares ~/.atlas/ with the CLI — no separate setup needed. See the WebUI section for the security model, daemon mode, and a walkthrough of the pages.

Upgrading to a newer version

When a new version is available, activate the venv and use --force-reinstall --no-compile instead of a plain pip install -U:

source ~/atlas_venv/bin/activate

# Upgrade the CLI
pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas-<version>-py3-none-any.whl

# Also upgrade the WebUI if you have it installed
pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas_webui-<version>-py3-none-any.whl

A plain pip install -U replaces source files but doesn't reliably clean up .pyc bytecode from the previous version. On RHEL and NFS-mounted filesystems in particular, stale bytecode can survive and cause confusing import errors or silently run old code.

FlagWhat it does
--force-reinstallForces a full remove-and-reinstall even if the version number hasn't changed. Orphaned files from the old version are cleaned up.
--no-compileSkips pre-generating .pyc bytecode during install. Python generates it fresh on first run, so stale bytecode can never coexist with new source files.
First run after upgrading will be slightly slower. Because --no-compile defers bytecode compilation, the very first invocation after an upgrade takes a second or two longer while Python builds the cache. This is a one-time cost.
✓
Your data is safe. Upgrading never touches ~/.atlas/ — your environments, sessions, captured data, and configuration are always preserved.

First-Time Setup

The first time you run platform-atlas with no configuration, it launches an interactive setup wizard. You can also run it at any time with:

platform-atlas config init

The wizard has two phases. Here's what to expect at each step.

1
Global Settings

You'll set your organization name (appears on reports and serves as the default for new environments), your preferred color theme, and a couple of optional settings. These are saved to ~/.atlas/config.json and apply across all environments.

2
First Environment

An environment represents one IAP deployment — for example, "production" or "dev". The wizard walks you through three things:

  • Credential storage — Choose between the OS keyring (default) and HashiCorp Vault. See the Vault section for details if your organization manages secrets in Vault.
  • Connection credentials — Your Platform URI, OAuth client ID, Platform client secret, MongoDB URI, and Redis URI. All stored securely in your chosen backend, never in config files.
  • Deployment topology — Tell Atlas how your environment is laid out: Standalone, HA2 (multiple nodes), Kubernetes (the wizard reads values.yaml directly), or Custom. For each server you pick a transport: SSH (default, key-based), ControlMaster when direct SSH is blocked by CyberArk PSMP or a jump host (works for any node — IAP, MongoDB, Redis, Gateway), or Local when Atlas itself is installed on the IAP server. You can leave an SSH destination blank and fill it in later — the wizard will warn but continue. See the ControlMaster section for details, and the SSH_SETUP_GUIDE.md companion guide for SSH setup.
At the end of setup, you'll be asked if you want to create another environment. If you manage dev, staging, and production deployments, set them all up now — or add them later with platform-atlas env create.

Environments

An environment is a named file that holds all the connection details and topology for one IAP deployment. You can have as many as you need — one per customer, one per deployment stage, whatever makes sense for your work.

Environment files live at ~/.atlas/environments/<name>.json. They store things like your Platform URI, OAuth client ID, deployment topology, and which credential backend to use. Sensitive values (passwords, URIs) are never written to the file — they stay in your keyring or Vault, scoped under platform-atlas/<env-name> so each environment's secrets are fully isolated.

Managing Environments

# See all environments (shows which is active; ⚠ incomplete = setup was interrupted)
platform-atlas env list

# Create a new environment (interactive wizard)
# A draft is saved early — Ctrl-C won't lose your work
platform-atlas env create

# If setup was interrupted, resume where you left off
platform-atlas env edit incomplete-env-name

# Copy an existing environment and adjust it
platform-atlas env create staging --from production

# Switch the active environment
platform-atlas env switch staging

# View details of an environment
platform-atlas env show production

# Edit settings (org name, URIs, topology)
# Topology opens a sub-menu: Edit a node / Change scope / Replace topology
platform-atlas env edit staging

# Remove an environment
platform-atlas env remove dev

Editing Topology Without Re-Running the Full Wizard

Running env edit and selecting Deployment Topology now opens a sub-menu with three options:

  • Edit a node — pick any node from the list and change its hostname, transport type (SSH / ControlMaster / Local), ControlMaster socket path, ControlMaster SSH destination, or SSH username. This is the right tool when you just need to fix one setting — for example, updating a hostname after a server migration or entering a ControlMaster SSH destination that was left blank during initial setup.
  • Change capture scope — toggle between primary_only (connect only to the primary node of each role — the default) and all_nodes (connect to every node in the topology). This does not affect node configuration, only which nodes Atlas visits during capture.
  • Replace topology — re-runs the full topology wizard from scratch. Use this when the deployment architecture itself has changed (e.g. upgrading from standalone to HA2).

One-off overrides

Use the --env flag to run a single command against a different environment without changing your active one:

platform-atlas --env dev preflight
platform-atlas --env staging session run capture
Environment resolution orderWhen Atlas starts, it looks for the active environment in this order: the --env flag → the ATLAS_ENV environment variable → the active_environment field in config.json → no environment (legacy mode).

ControlMaster Transport (CyberArk PSMP / Jump Hosts)

When SSH to a server requires MFA or is routed through a PAM gateway like CyberArk PSMP, Atlas uses ControlMaster transport — it piggybacks on a single pre-authenticated SSH session you open before capture, eliminating repeated MFA prompts. ControlMaster can be applied to any node independently: IAP, MongoDB, Redis, or Gateway.

How It Works

You open one SSH master connection per role (completing MFA once per node). Atlas then multiplexes all of its collection commands through those open sockets — no new TCP connections, no further authentication. The sockets are stored under ~/.atlas/sockets/ with short, role-based names that stay well under the POSIX 104-byte socket path limit.

Step 1 — Open the Master Connections

Before running session run capture, open one master connection per role that uses ControlMaster transport:

# Platform / IAP node
ssh -M -S ~/.atlas/sockets/platform-01.sock \
    -o ControlPersist=10m \
    -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \
    -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
    -fN user@iap-host@psmp-gateway.example.com

# MongoDB primary (Extended tier only)
ssh -M -S ~/.atlas/sockets/mongo-01.sock \
    -o ControlPersist=10m \
    -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \
    -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
    -fN user@mongo-host@psmp-gateway.example.com

# Redis primary (Extended tier only)
ssh -M -S ~/.atlas/sockets/redis-01.sock \
    -o ControlPersist=10m \
    -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \
    -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
    -fN user@redis-host@psmp-gateway.example.com

The exact commands for your environment are shown by env sockets — see below. Atlas shows them again at capture time if any socket is missing.

HA2: one socket per role, not one per node. Atlas only SSH-connects to the primary node of each role in the default primary_only capture scope. You only need to open master connections for the primary IAP, primary MongoDB, and primary Redis — not for every HA2 member.

Step 2 — Configure the Environment

During env create or env edit, when you select ControlMaster as a node's transport, Atlas asks for:

  • Socket path — auto-suggested (e.g. ~/.atlas/sockets/platform-01.sock); customize if needed
  • SSH destination — the full target string for the ssh -M command (e.g. user@iap-host@psmp-gateway.example.com)
  • Port — SSH port for the master connection (default 22)

You can leave the SSH destination blank if you don't have it yet — the wizard will warn but continue. Fill it in later with env edit → Deployment Topology → Edit a node.

Step 3 — Check Socket Health

# Show status of all ControlMaster sockets for an environment
platform-atlas env sockets production

# Clean up stale socket files (socket exists but master is not responding)
platform-atlas env sockets production --clean

Socket statuses:

  • ✔ open — socket is valid and the master is responding
  • ⚠ stale — socket file exists but the master connection has closed; run --clean then re-open
  • ✘ not found — socket was never opened; run the ssh -M -S … command shown
  • — no SSH dest — SSH destination was left blank during setup; fix with env edit → Edit a node

Step 4 — Run Atlas

With sockets open, run capture normally:

platform-atlas session run capture

If any sockets are missing or stale, Atlas shows the status table and asks whether to proceed. Nodes without open sockets fail individually — they do not abort the entire capture. You can re-open missing sockets and re-run; Atlas resumes from the checkpoint.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause Fix
socket exists but is not responding Stale socket — master timed out or was closed env sockets <name> --clean, then re-open the master
filename too long / bind error Socket path exceeds the 104-byte POSIX limit Use the default short paths under ~/.atlas/sockets/
SSH destination not configured for node X Node saved without an SSH destination env edit → Deployment Topology → Edit a node → CM SSH destination
Socket shows missing at capture time Master was never opened for this session Run the ssh -M -S … command shown by env sockets

Running an Audit

An audit in Atlas follows a fixed sequence. Each step feeds into the next, and all the results from a single audit live together in a session — a named directory under ~/.atlas/sessions/.

1

Preflight

Before you collect anything, verify that Atlas can reach everything it needs to. Preflight tests each service independently and tells you exactly what passed, failed, or was skipped.

platform-atlas preflight

It checks SSH connectivity to all nodes, MongoDB and Redis authentication, Platform API reachability, and config file readability. Fix any failures before continuing — a capture with missing connectivity will produce an incomplete dataset.

For a broader configuration health check that also covers credential presence, ruleset state, and SSH key path, use:

platform-atlas config doctor

config doctor verifies the global config, active environment, credential backend, Platform / Gateway URL reachability, active ruleset, and SSH key path in a single pass. Each row prints a ✓ OK, ⚠ warning, or ✗ error with a fix-it suggestion when something is wrong. Exit codes: 0 OK, 1 warnings, 2 errors — composes cleanly with CI gates.

2

Create a Session

A session binds together an environment, a ruleset, and a profile — and holds all the files for one complete audit. When you switch sessions later, the full context switches with it.

# Interactive — walks you through environment, ruleset, and profile
platform-atlas session create prod-audit-q1

# Or specify everything upfront
platform-atlas session create prod-audit-q1 \
  --env production \
  --ruleset p6-master-ruleset \
  --profile p6-prod-standalone-gateway4

The session becomes active immediately after creation. If you made a mistake (wrong environment, wrong profile), you can fix it with platform-atlas session edit — but only before capture begins.

3

Capture

This is where Atlas goes out and collects data. You'll see a live progress display as each collector runs — system info, MongoDB status, Redis config, Platform API health, log files, and more. If one collector fails, the rest keep going.

platform-atlas session run capture

If a collector fails, Atlas offers a guided fallback to let you provide the data manually. Skip it with --skip-guided if you don't need it. You can also batch-import pre-collected files for air-gapped environments:

platform-atlas session run capture --manual --import-dir ~/atlas-files/

After capture completes, Atlas will ask if you want to run MongoDB aggregation pipelines for the operational report. These query live workflow and task data — accept if you want execution statistics in the report, decline if you only need the compliance data.

4

Validate

Validation runs your captured data through every rule in the active ruleset. Each rule produces a PASS, FAIL, SKIP, or ERROR result. Rules can depend on other rules — if a dependency fails, downstream rules are automatically skipped rather than producing misleading errors.

platform-atlas session run validate

After the primary ruleset runs, Atlas runs a set of Extended Validation checks that analyze patterns across the full dataset — adapter version coverage, log error rates, Redis ACL completeness, and more.

5

Report

Generates three HTML reports in one pass and opens the compliance report in your browser.

platform-atlas session run report
FileContents
03_report.htmlCompliance score, category breakdown, all rule results, extended validation findings
04_operational.htmlPlatform, webserver, and MongoDB log analysis; MongoDB pipeline metrics
05_arch.htmlAdapter states, Redis ACL, index status, IAG paths, architecture overview

All three reports share a header navigation bar so you can switch between them without leaving your browser. If you're on a headless server, find the reports at ~/.atlas/sessions/<name>/ and copy them to your local machine.

Run everything at once

Once you're comfortable with the workflow, run all three stages in one command:

platform-atlas session run all

Add --headless for automated or scripted runs — it suppresses all interactive prompts, guided fallbacks, and won't try to open a browser:

platform-atlas session run all --headless

Filtering log dates

You can narrow the log collection window during capture using date flags:

# Collect logs for a specific date range
platform-atlas session run capture --log-since 2026-04-01 --log-until 2026-04-21

When a date range is used, the operational report shows a banner indicating which window was captured. Normal capture behavior is unchanged when neither flag is provided.

Managing Sessions

Sessions are the primary unit of organization in Atlas. Each one represents a complete audit cycle and carries its own environment, ruleset, profile, and organization name — switching sessions restores the full context in one step.

Switching sessions

# Interactive picker — shows environment, org, and status for each
platform-atlas session switch

# Or switch directly by name
platform-atlas session switch prod-audit-q1

Viewing sessions

platform-atlas session list                     # All sessions with status
platform-atlas session show                     # Details of the active session
platform-atlas session show prod-audit-q1       # Details of a specific session

Editing session bindings

Made a mistake during session creation? You can change the environment, ruleset, or profile — but only before capture begins. Once capture starts, the session is locked to protect data consistency.

platform-atlas session edit

Comparing sessions

If you've run audits at different times, compare them to see exactly what changed:

platform-atlas session diff baseline-q4 current-q1

The diff report classifies each rule as Fixed, Regressed, Unchanged, New, Removed, or Skipped. It's the fastest way to demonstrate progress to stakeholders or catch regressions after a configuration change.

Exporting sessions

platform-atlas session export prod-audit-q1

This creates a ZIP archive containing the reports, session metadata, and a README. Raw capture data is redacted by default — add --no-redact if you need the full JSON for troubleshooting.

Cleaning up

# Delete a specific session
platform-atlas session delete prod-audit-q1

# Bulk-delete uncaptured sessions older than 30 days
platform-atlas session prune --older-than 30
platform-atlas session prune --older-than 30 --dry-run   # Preview first

Rulesets & Profiles

A ruleset is the "answer key" for what a healthy deployment should look like. Atlas ships with the Platform 6 Master Ruleset containing 105 rules across five categories.

CategoryRulesCoverage
Platform47Application settings, adapters, services, properties
Gateway523IAG5 configuration, health, version checks
Redis16Server config, memory, persistence, replication, ACLs
Gateway411Venv packages, sync config, database settings
MongoDB8Server status, version, replication, connection settings

The easiest way to select a ruleset and profile is the interactive setup command — it walks you through both in one step and is the recommended approach when creating sessions:

platform-atlas ruleset setup

Profiles

Profiles are lightweight overlays that enable or disable specific rules for a particular environment type. Instead of maintaining separate rulesets for every configuration, you pick a profile that matches your deployment.

ProfileUse for
p6-prod-standalone-gateway4Production standalone with Gateway4
p6-prod-standalone-gateway5Production standalone with Gateway5
p6-prod-standalone-no-gatewayProduction standalone, no gateway
p6-prod-ha2-gateway4Production HA2 with Gateway4
p6-prod-ha2-gateway5Production HA2 with Gateway5
p6-dev-standalone-gateway4Development standalone with Gateway4
p6-dev-standalone-gateway5Development standalone with Gateway5
 
# List available profiles
platform-atlas ruleset profile list

# Set a profile
platform-atlas ruleset profile set p6-prod-ha2-gateway4

# Check what's active
platform-atlas ruleset active
platform-atlas ruleset profile active

HashiCorp Vault Integration

If your organization manages secrets in Vault, Atlas can read credentials from a KV v2 secrets engine instead of the OS keyring. Atlas is strictly read-only — it never writes to Vault. Your team manages the actual secrets through the Vault UI, CLI, or API.

Vault connection settings (URL, auth method, path) are stored in the OS keyring under a vault_ prefix, keeping them off disk entirely. The actual credentials Atlas uses to run audits (Platform secret, MongoDB URI, etc.) live in Vault at your configured path.

To configure Vault as your credential backend during setup, select it when the wizard asks. To reconfigure an existing installation:

platform-atlas config credentials

Choosing an auth method

Atlas supports five authentication methods, split into two groups. If your organization's security policy doesn't require credential rotation, either Standard method is a fine choice. If credentials rotate automatically — or if you want them to — use one of the Automated methods.

Token Standard

You provide a Vault token directly. Atlas stores it in the OS keyring and uses it on every run.

Good for simple setups where the token is long-lived or you rotate it manually.

AppRole Standard

You provide a role_id and a static secret_id. Atlas stores both in the OS keyring and uses them to authenticate on every run.

Good for machine-to-machine authentication when the secret_id doesn't need to rotate.

AppRole (Wrapped) Automated

Instead of a raw secret_id, you store a wrapping token — a one-time-use token that Vault unwraps to retrieve the actual secret_id at connect time. The token is consumed on first use, so a stolen keyring entry can't be reused after Atlas has run.

Your pipeline or Vault admin generates a fresh wrapping token on a schedule and updates the keyring entry. Atlas handles the unwrap transparently.

Good when your security policy requires rotating secret_ids but you can't run a daemon on the Atlas host.

Token (file) Automated

Atlas reads a token from a file on disk at runtime. Vault Agent — a separate service from HashiCorp — runs on the same host, authenticates to Vault independently, and writes a continuously-renewed token to that file. You configure the file path once; after that, Atlas always finds a valid token with zero maintenance on your part.

The best fully-automated option. Set it up once with your Vault admin, then never think about credential rotation again. See Vault Agent Setup below.

Token (env) Automated

Atlas reads the VAULT_TOKEN environment variable at runtime. Nothing is stored in Atlas — your pipeline, systemd unit, or orchestrator is responsible for setting that variable before Atlas runs.

Good for CI/CD pipelines or orchestrated environments that already manage Vault tokens and inject them as environment variables.

Setting up Vault Agent (Token file method)

Vault Agent is a separate binary that HashiCorp distributes with Vault. Your Vault admin sets it up once on the Atlas host:

1

Install Vault Agent

Download and install the Vault binary from HashiCorp. The same binary serves as both the server and the agent.

2

Write an agent config file

Create a config file (e.g. /etc/vault-agent/atlas.hcl) with an auto_auth block pointing to your Vault instance and a sink block specifying the token file path:

vault {
  address = "https://vault.yourcompany.com:8200"
}

auto_auth {
  method "approle" {
    config = {
      role_id_file_path   = "/etc/vault-agent/role_id"
      secret_id_file_path = "/etc/vault-agent/secret_id"
    }
  }
}

sink "file" {
  path = "/run/vault-agent/atlas.token"
}
3

Run as a systemd service

Create a systemd unit so the agent starts at boot and stays running. Vault Agent automatically renews the token before it expires and re-authenticates if it ever expires.

4

Configure Atlas

Run platform-atlas config credentials, select Token (file), and enter the sink path (/run/vault-agent/atlas.token). Atlas will read a valid token from that file every time it runs — no further maintenance needed.

Troubleshooting Vault

"Vault unreachable" or "Credential Backend Failed"Atlas can't connect to Vault. Verify Vault is running and the URL is correct, then check the method-specific details below.
MethodCommon causeFix
tokenToken expiredRun config credentials and enter a new token
approleSecret ID expired or revokedRun config credentials and re-enter role_id and secret_id
approle_wrappedWrapping token already used or expiredObtain a fresh wrapping token from your pipeline or Vault admin, then run config credentials
token_fileVault Agent not running or path wrongCheck that the agent service is active and writing to the configured path
token_envVAULT_TOKEN not setEnsure the environment variable is set before running Atlas

Vault secrets path

Your Atlas credentials should be stored in Vault as key-value pairs at the configured path (default: secret/data/platform-atlas):

Vault keyDescription
platform_client_secretPlatform OAuth client secret (required)
mongo_uriMongoDB connection URI
redis_uriRedis connection URI
ssh_key_passphraseSSH key passphrase (if applicable)
gateway4_passwordGateway4 API password (if applicable)

Continuous Audit & Fleet (new in v1.7)

A formal session run is a point-in-time snapshot. Continuous Audit fills the gap between formal runs by re-executing a Platform-OAuth-only capture against the active ruleset on a schedule and recording any rule whose observed value drifted from the prior run as an alert. Captures are locked to Platform OAuth regardless of tier, so it works in Standard and Extended without any extra access.

Getting started

Before you enable the schedule, run one capture by hand to confirm the OAuth path works and seed the prior-run state:

platform-atlas continuous-audit run-once
platform-atlas continuous-audit enable     # installs systemd-user / launchd timer
platform-atlas continuous-audit status     # last run, next run, alert counts

Alerts and ack

When a rule's observed value changes between runs, Atlas opens an alert. Alerts persist until you ack them, and re-open if drift recurs after an ack.

platform-atlas continuous-audit alerts
platform-atlas continuous-audit ack <alert-id>
platform-atlas continuous-audit ack --all

Policy and watchlist

Default policy is any — every state change is an alert. Switch to regression when you only want PASS → FAIL transitions. The watchlist filters notifications and the alert UI down to specific rule numbers; everything still goes to the events.ndjson timeline.

platform-atlas continuous-audit policy regression
platform-atlas continuous-audit watch add 12 47 102
platform-atlas continuous-audit watch list

Notifications

Per-environment Slack and webhook channels deliver alert-state transitions. Notifications fire only on newly opened alerts and re-opened alerts after ack — persistent unacked drift won't spam.

platform-atlas continuous-audit notify add slack
platform-atlas continuous-audit notify add webhook    # with optional HMAC-SHA256 signing
platform-atlas continuous-audit notify test <id>
Payloads carry rule identity onlyNotification bodies include the rule number, name, severity, and alert ID — never the previous or current observed values. A misconfigured Slack/webhook channel cannot exfiltrate captured Platform secrets.

Fleet view

The fleet command is a read-only overview of every environment Atlas knows about. It reads the local cache only — it never triggers a capture or hits the Platform API.

platform-atlas fleet status
platform-atlas fleet status --json

For each environment you'll see the current tier, most recent session and its age, pass rate, continuous-audit state, and unacked alert count. The same data renders at /fleet in the WebUI as a sortable card grid.

WebUI (new optional package)

The optional platform-atlas-webui 1.0.0 wheel is a browser-based interface for the same workflow you use in the CLI. It's a thin presentation layer over the same engines — both interfaces read and write the same ~/.atlas/ directory; what you do in one shows up in the other immediately.

The WebUI is local-only — it serves on localhost over self-signed TLS and authenticates the OS user that started it. There is no remote / multi-tenant deployment mode.

Installing and first launch

pip install platform_atlas_webui-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
platform-atlas-webui

On first launch Atlas writes a self-signed TLS certificate to ~/.atlas/.webui-cert.pem, prints its SHA-256 fingerprint, and opens your default browser at a one-time nonce-signed login URL. The first request consumes the nonce and sets a signed session cookie; subsequent navigation just works.

If Atlas has never been set up before, the WebUI redirects to /setup and walks you through the same wizard you'd see in platform-atlas config init.

Daemon mode

For an always-on local install, run detached:

platform-atlas-webui --daemon       # double-fork; PID at ~/.atlas/webui.pid
platform-atlas-webui status
platform-atlas-webui restart
platform-atlas-webui stop
platform-atlas-webui login-url      # mint a fresh URL after restart

Daemon mode supports Linux and macOS. On Windows, run the foreground command in a terminal you keep open.

Security model

LayerWhat it does
TLSSelf-signed cert at ~/.atlas/.webui-cert.pem; regenerate with --reset-tls. Browsers warn the first time — accept for localhost.
OS-user bindingToken file at ~/.atlas/.webui-token (mode 0600). Browser session cookies are signed against that token plus a separate cookie secret. Rotating either invalidates every outstanding cookie (--reset-token).
CSRFStateless HMAC tokens injected into every form, required on AJAX POST / PATCH / DELETE.
CSP & headersStrict response headers. HTML reports themselves render under a sandboxed CSP — captured data cannot reach back into the WebUI's authenticated origin.
Audit logEvery state-changing request appends one JSON line to ~/.atlas/webui-audit.log (rotates at 10 MB).

Page-by-page tour

PageWhat you do here
/ DashboardKPI tiles, audit-activity heatmap of the last 48 h, zero-state helpers when tiles are empty.
/sessionsCreate, activate, run capture/validate/report. Live SSE output stream; force-kill button after 60 s.
/environmentsCreate, edit, activate, delete environments. Activation atomically restores tier, ruleset, and profile alongside the env.
/credentialsReconfigure Keyring vs Vault for the active env. All five Vault auth methods supported including AppRole-Wrapped, Token (file), Token (env).
/reportsDirect links to every session's compliance, operational, and architecture HTML reports.
/tierSide-by-side cards for Standard and Extended; switch with a confirmation modal.
/fleetSortable card grid mirroring fleet status — read-only, never triggers a capture.
/continuousStatus, settings, run history. Alerting block with alert_policy selector and watchlist chip editor.
/alertsDrift timeline with ack and ack-all. Bell icon in the topbar shows unacked count.
/notificationsAdd, edit, test, and remove Slack and webhook channels. HMAC signing toggle.
/settingsTheme picker (Aurora / Horizon palettes), light/dark mode segmented control.

Themes

Theme palette and light/dark mode are independent axes:

  • Aurora — confident, technical (deep navy + electric blue). Default.
  • Horizon — warm, editorial (charcoal + terracotta).

The moon/sun toggle in the topbar swaps light/dark and preserves your palette choice. Settings persist in config.json under webui_theme, webui_accent, and webui_mode.

Troubleshooting

Atlas writes a log to ~/.atlas/atlas.log. For verbose output during a command, add --debug:

platform-atlas --debug session run capture

Common issues

ErrorFix
"Config file not found"Run platform-atlas config init to create the initial configuration.
"No ruleset loaded"Switch to the session with session switch to restore its bound ruleset, or run ruleset setup.
"Connection refused" during preflightVerify the host is reachable, the correct port is open, and the SSH user has key-based access.
"Insecure keyring backend"Install a supported backend. On headless Linux: pip install keyrings.alt, or switch to Vault.
"Permission denied" on config fileRun chmod 600 ~/.atlas/config.json
"Environment not found"Run platform-atlas env list to see available environments.
Capture module fails, others succeedExpected — Atlas continues with remaining modules. Use --skip-guided to suppress fallback prompts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I run Atlas against a production system safely?

Yes. Atlas is strictly read-only. It reads config files via SSH and uses read-only API operations on MongoDB, Redis, and Platform. It never modifies configuration, restarts services, or writes data to your IAP environment.

Some collectors failed during capture. Is my data incomplete?

Partial captures are completely normal. Atlas is designed to work with whatever it can collect. Failed collectors show as SKIP in the report, and the compliance score is calculated only against rules that had actual data to evaluate. If you have pre-collected files for the failed modules, import them with --manual --import-dir.

I have dev, staging, and production deployments. Do I need separate Atlas installations?

No — create an environment for each one, then create sessions bound to each environment. Switching between audits is a single platform-atlas session switch command.

I upgraded from a version before 1.5. Do I need to redo my setup?

No. Existing configurations, sessions, and environments all continue to work. Sessions created before v1.5 won't have bound rulesets or environments — they'll use whatever is globally active. You can backfill metadata with platform-atlas session repair.

Where does Atlas store its data?

~/.atlas/
├── config.json          # Global settings (no secrets)
├── atlas.log            # Application log
├── environments/        # One JSON file per deployment target
├── sessions/            # One folder per audit session
│   └── prod-audit-q1/
│       ├── session.json
│       ├── 01_capture.json
│       ├── 02_validation.parquet
│       ├── 03_report.html
│       ├── 04_operational.html
│       └── 05_arch.html
└── pipelines/           # Custom MongoDB pipeline definitions

I need to run Atlas on a schedule

Use --headless to suppress all interactive prompts, and pre-create a named session for the scheduled run:

platform-atlas session run all --headless

Make sure your credential backend works non-interactively. On Linux, this means either keyrings.alt (encrypted file backend) or Vault with the token_file or token_env auth method.

That's everything!If something isn't covered here, see the Itential support documentation.

Platform Atlas — User Guide

Installation & Usage Guide

Everything you need to get from a fresh install to a full compliance report — step by step, with no prior Platform Atlas experience required.

Installation

Up and running in minutes

Platform Atlas ships as a Python wheel (.whl) file provided by your Itential contact. You need Python 3.11 or newer — that's the only requirement. The easiest way to install is the install script included in the install_scripts/ folder: it checks your Python version, creates a virtual environment, installs Atlas (and optionally the WebUI), and wires up your shell so platform-atlas works from any terminal.

# macOS / Linux — run from the folder containing the wheel
$ bash install_scripts/linux-mac_install.sh
✓ Found Python 3.11.9
✓ Found wheel: platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
✓ Virtual environment created at ~/atlas_venv
✓ Installed successfully: platform-atlas 2.0.0
$ platform-atlas --version
platform-atlas 2.0.0 · Python 3.11.9

Prefer to do it manually? Create a venv with python3.11 -m venv ~/atlas_venv, activate it, and pip install --force-reinstall --no-compile platform_atlas-*.whl. See the Installation section in the User Guide tab for OS-specific Python install instructions and a troubleshooting table.

First-Time Setup

One wizard, everything configured

The first time you run platform-atlas it detects no configuration and launches an interactive setup wizard. You can also run it any time with platform-atlas config init.

The wizard has two phases. Phase 1 captures global settings — your organization name and theme. Phase 2 creates your first environment: credentials for IAP, MongoDB, and Redis (stored in your OS keyring, never in plain text), and your deployment topology (standalone, HA2, or custom) including SSH access details for each server.

When the wizard finishes, you're ready to run your first preflight check.

Sessions

One session, full context

In Platform Atlas, a session is the central unit of work. When you create a session, you bind three things to it: the environment to audit, the ruleset (the set of validation rules), and the profile (a deployment-specific overlay like 'standalone' or 'ha2-with-gateway').

Those bindings are locked in. Switch to a different session and all three switch automatically — no more forgetting to change the ruleset when you switch environments. Sessions also track your progress through the pipeline: capture, validate, report.

  • Create a session with platform-atlas session create
  • Switch with session switch
  • Edit bindings (before capture) with session edit
Running an Audit

Four commands. One complete audit.

Once a session is created, auditing your deployment is a four-step pipeline. Capture connects to every server and service in your deployment and collects configuration data — IAP API responses, MongoDB server status, Redis CONFIG, Gateway runtime data, SSH config files, and log samples.

Validate evaluates that data against every rule in your ruleset, producing PASS, FAIL, SKIP, or ERROR results for each. Report generates all three HTML reports in one pass — compliance (03_report.html), operational (04_operational.html), and architecture (05_arch.html) — and opens the compliance report in your browser.

Or run all three at once: platform-atlas session run all

Preflight checks

Before your first audit, run platform-atlas preflight to test connectivity to every service — IAP API, MongoDB, Redis, SSH targets, and config files. It tells you exactly what failed and why.

Rulesets and profiles

A ruleset is the set of best-practice rules Atlas validates against. A profile is a deployment-specific overlay (standalone, HA2, HA2 with Gateway). Both are bound to your session at creation.

Multiple environments

Create an environment for each deployment — dev, staging, production. Each has its own credentials, topology, and organization name. Sessions tie to a specific environment, so switching is always clean.

⚡

Headless and automated

For cron jobs or CI pipelines, use --headless to suppress all interactive prompts. Combine with --import-dir to batch-import pre-collected files without any interaction.

Session Management

Switch, compare, and share

As you build up sessions over time, Atlas gives you tools to manage them. session list shows all sessions with their environment, status, and progress.

session switch restores the full context of any previous session — environment, ruleset, and profile all switch with it. session diff compares two sessions and generates an HTML comparison report highlighting rules that improved or regressed. session export packages the report and metadata into a ZIP for sharing.

  • Workstation setup
  • IAP OAuth credentials

Selected
You can switch tiers at any time — the checklist updates instantly. If you're unsure, start with Standard. Auditing a standalone gateway with no Platform? That's the SaaS tier — chosen per-environment in env create; it needs only gateway credentials (see the Tiers section).
Required
Workstation
Why we need this

Atlas is a CLI tool that runs on your machine — not on your servers. Your workstation is the control plane for every audit.

What it unlocks

A supported Python version and pip allow Atlas to install and run correctly. The .whl file is Atlas itself. A secure credential backend means Atlas can store sensitive secrets — OAuth tokens, database URIs, SSH passphrases — without ever writing them to a plain-text config file.

Without it

Atlas cannot be installed or launched. Without a credential backend, secrets would need to be re-entered every session and could not be stored securely between runs.

Required
Itential Automation Platform (IAP)
Why we need this

IAP is the primary system being audited. Atlas authenticates using OAuth2 — the Client ID and Secret let it obtain short-lived access tokens to call IAP's REST API. This is strictly a read-only connection: Atlas never modifies IAP configuration or state.

What it unlocks

Atlas can collect the IAP platform version, installed application inventory, active services, and runtime configuration directly from the live system. This data forms the backbone of the compliance report and is required for the majority of ruleset evaluations.

Without it

The IAP audit cannot run at all. Every IAP-related rule — the large majority of the ruleset — will be unevaluable. Without IAP data, the compliance report is not meaningful.

SSH Access — IAP Nodes
Required for full audit
MongoDB
Why we need this

MongoDB is IAP's primary persistent data store. Atlas connects using the pymongo driver to run read-only diagnostic commands — the same ones a DBA would use to inspect server health. No application data or IAP-owned collection contents are ever read.

What it unlocks

Atlas can validate MongoDB's authentication mode, TLS configuration, journaling, oplog size, replica set health, and storage-layer settings that directly affect IAP's data integrity and availability under load.

Without it

All MongoDB-related rules will show as SKIP in the report. Misconfigurations such as disabled authentication or an undersized oplog won't surface — you lose all visibility into storage-layer compliance.

SSH Access — MongoDB Nodes
ℹ️ MongoDB auditing can be skipped if not needed — leave the URI blank during Atlas setup and MongoDB-related rules will show as SKIP in the report.
Required for full audit
Redis
Why we need this

Redis is IAP's real-time message broker, task queue, and session cache. Atlas connects via redis-py to read server configuration using CONFIG GET — it does not read application data, keys, or values stored by IAP.

What it unlocks

Atlas can validate Redis settings including maxmemory policy, persistence mode (AOF/RDB), bind address, TLS configuration, and ACL setup — all settings that affect IAP's job scheduling, event handling, and session reliability.

Without it

All Redis-related rules will show as SKIP. Redis misconfigurations that could cause IAP job failures, session drops, or data loss under memory pressure won't surface in the report.

SSH Access — Redis Nodes
ℹ️ Like MongoDB, Redis auditing can be skipped by leaving the URI blank during setup. Redis rules will appear as SKIP in the report.
Required
Deployment Topology
Why we need this

Before Atlas can connect to anything, it needs a map of your environment. Topology defines which hosts run which services, how they relate to each other, and what deployment mode your installation uses. Without this map, Atlas doesn't know where to send connections.

What it unlocks

Atlas builds its entire capture plan from the topology — which hosts to SSH into for each role, which addresses to connect to for MongoDB and Redis, and which nodes are primary vs. secondary. This drives the full audit workflow from initial capture through to report generation.

Without it

Atlas cannot run a capture. Topology is not optional infrastructure detail — it is fundamental configuration Atlas requires before doing any work. An incorrect topology means Atlas will connect to the wrong hosts or miss entire services entirely.

Optional
Automation Gateway 4
Why we need this

Automation Gateway 4 is the REST API-based gateway service for IAP integrations. If it's present in your deployment, it has its own configuration that Atlas audits separately from IAP core. Atlas queries the Gateway 4 API directly because automation-gateway.db is the authoritative configuration source — the properties.yml file on disk can be stale after first boot.

What it unlocks

Atlas can capture Gateway 4's runtime configuration, installed version, enabled integrations, and connectivity settings — validating them against the same ruleset that governs the rest of your deployment. API-sourced data is more reliable than reading config files directly.

Without it

If you have Gateway 4 deployed but skip this section, all Gateway 4 rules will show as SKIP and your report will have a gap in gateway coverage. If you genuinely don't use Gateway 4, checking the skip toggle below has no effect on the rest of the audit.

ℹ️ Gateway 4 uses a REST API as its primary data source. Atlas reads automation-gateway.db via GET /config — the properties.yml file on disk may be stale after first boot and is only used as a fallback if the API is unreachable.
Optional
Automation Gateway 5
Why we need this

Automation Gateway 5 is the newer Python-based gateway. Unlike Gateway 4, it has no REST API — all of its configuration is read via SSH by inspecting the virtual environment and reading environment variables from the service unit. Atlas uses the same SSH connection already established for the core audit.

What it unlocks

Atlas can report the installed Gateway 5 package version and validate its environment configuration, ensuring the settings meet compatibility requirements for your IAP version. No additional ports or credentials are required beyond the SSH setup covered in the Platform, MongoDB, and Redis sections.

Without it

If you have Gateway 5 deployed but skip this section, all Gateway 5 rules will show as SKIP and your report will have a gap in gateway coverage. The SSH user's read permissions simply need to cover the Gateway 5 virtual environment directory — no new network access is needed.

ℹ️ Gateway 5 is entirely SSH-based — there is no REST API to query. Atlas reads package version information and environment variables over the same SSH connection used for the rest of the audit. No additional network ports need to be opened beyond SSH.

You're ready to install Platform Atlas

All applicable prerequisites are confirmed. Run pip install platform_atlas-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl on your workstation to get started, then follow the Installation & Usage Guide to configure your first environment and run your first audit.

Platform Atlas — User Guide

Review Compliance Report for Actionable Insights

Every number, status, and finding explained — plus practical examples showing exactly how to fix what the report surfaces.

Report Layout

Four sections, one complete picture

The Platform Atlas HTML report is self-contained — open it in any browser, no internet required. It has four main sections working top-to-bottom.

The compliance score gives you the headline number and a per-category breakdown. The results table lists every rule evaluated in this session with its status and message. Extended validation surfaces pattern-based findings that single-value rules can't catch — things like log error rate trends and adapter version consistency. Log analysis shows the most frequent error patterns from Platform application logs during the capture window.

Compliance Score

The score tells you where you stand

The compliance score at the top of the report is the percentage of evaluated rules that passed. Rules marked SKIP — which happens when data couldn't be collected for a service — are excluded from both the numerator and denominator. So a 90% score on 80 evaluated rules means the same thing as a 90% score on 60 rules: 90% of what Atlas could check, passed.

The score is broken down by category — Platform, MongoDB, Redis, Gateway4, and Gateway5 — so you can immediately see which area needs the most attention. Target 90% or above on all categories for a healthy production deployment.

Rule Statuses

Four outcomes, clear meaning

Every rule in the results table has one of four statuses. PASS means the rule evaluated and the configuration met the expected value — nothing to do. FAIL means the rule evaluated but the configuration does not meet the expected value — this needs attention, and the message in the report explains exactly what was found and why it matters.

SKIP means data wasn't available to evaluate the rule — this is common when a service was unreachable during capture or when a rule doesn't apply to this deployment type. SKIP is not the same as PASS. ERROR means the rule evaluation itself failed, usually due to a type mismatch or version difference — report these to your Itential contact.

Severity Levels

Not all failures are equal

Every rule has a severity level that tells you how urgently a FAIL needs attention. Critical failures directly threaten data integrity, availability, or security — fix these before your next business cycle. Examples include an unhealthy MongoDB replica set, an incorrect Redis eviction policy, or an unsupported software version.

Warning failures represent configuration that deviates from best practice in ways that may cause problems under load or over time — address these in your next planned maintenance window. Info failures are observations with low immediate risk: default accounts still active, audit retention at default values, optional features not configured. Address these before compliance reviews.

Remediation

Read the message, apply the fix

Every FAIL in the report includes a plain-English message explaining what was found and why it matters. Here are three real examples with their fix steps.

RDS-002 Redis MaxMemory Policy Critical

“Redis maxmemory-policy is not set to noeviction — with other policies, Redis may silently evict important data when memory pressure increases.”

  1. Open the Redis configuration file at /etc/redis/redis.conf.
  2. Locate or add the maxmemory-policy directive.
  3. Set it to: maxmemory-policy noeviction
  4. Restart Redis to apply: sudo systemctl restart redis
  5. Verify the running value with: redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy
MDB-002 MongoDB Bind IP Warning

“MongoDB is bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) — this exposes the database to all network traffic and is a security risk in production.”

  1. Open the MongoDB configuration file at /etc/mongod.conf.
  2. Under the net: section, replace the wildcard with specific IPs: bindIp: 127.0.0.1,<platform-server-ip>
  3. Only include addresses required for Platform connectivity and local administration.
  4. Restart MongoDB to apply: sudo systemctl restart mongod
  5. Verify the binding with: ss -tlnp | grep 27017
IAG-003 Gateway HTTP Server Threads Critical

“HTTP server threads are below the recommended value of 3× the CPU core count — this can create a bottleneck under load and cause request timeouts.”

  1. Open the Automation Gateway properties.yml file.
  2. Calculate 3× the number of CPU cores on the server (e.g. 16 cores → 48 threads).
  3. Set http_server_threads to that value.
  4. Save the file and restart Automation Gateway: sudo systemctl restart automation-gateway

After fixing, re-run platform-atlas session run all to confirm the rules now pass.

Best Practices
Getting the most from your report

Prioritize by impact

Start with Critical FAILs that affect current availability (unhealthy replica sets, services down). Then address security (open bindings, default accounts). Then configuration correctness (thread counts, eviction policies). Info-level items last.

Share the report

The HTML report is self-contained — email it, drop it in a shared folder, or attach it to a ticket. To include session metadata, use platform-atlas session export which creates a redacted ZIP package.

Compare across audits

After making fixes, create a new session and run the full audit again. Then use platform-atlas session diff baseline-session follow-up-session to generate an HTML comparison showing exactly what improved, what regressed, and what stayed the same.

Export in other formats

Need the results in a spreadsheet or data pipeline? Use --format csv or --format json when generating the report. These exports include the environment name and all rule metadata alongside each result.
